seo.og_title: Grande Mosquée of Oujda (Al Kabir): History & Visit Tips
seo.og_description: The oldest mosque in Oujda’s medina – elegant minaret, three fountains and a calm spiritual heart of the old city.

name: Grande Mosquée (Al Kabir)
hero_subtitle: Oujda’s oldest mosque: a Marinid landmark with an elegant minaret and the famous three fountains at the edge of the medina.

info.entry_val: Exterior free; prayer times for Muslims

overview.title: The Spiritual Heart of the Old City
overview.p1: The Grande Mosquée, also known as Jamaa Al Kabir or Lkebir Jamaa, is the oldest major religious building in Oujda. Founded under the Marinid dynasty, it rises above the medina with a simple yet elegant minaret that has become one of the city’s visual landmarks.
overview.p2: Non-Muslims can admire the exterior and the three decorative fountains (Tlat Skaki) near the entrance, which are covered in colourful zellige. The area around the mosque is a natural pause point during a medina walk – quieter than the main commercial lanes yet full of local life.
overview.p3: It is not a museum; it remains an active place of worship. Respectful behaviour, modest dress and awareness of prayer times make a short visit both pleasant and appropriate.

moods.title: When to Visit the Grande Mosquée
moods.subtitle: A short stop that fits naturally into a medina morning or late afternoon.

1.title: Soft Light and Quiet Streets
1.desc: Best for photos of the minaret and fountains before the medina becomes busy. The light is gentle and the area feels calm.

2.title: Golden Hour Around the Mosque
2.desc: The stone and tiles catch warm light. Combine with a slow walk through nearby lanes and a stop for tea or karan.

3.title: Respect Active Worship
3.desc: Avoid lingering near entrances during the five daily prayers. Non-Muslims should stay outside the prayer hall at all times.

food.title: What to Eat Nearby
food.p1: The lanes around the mosque are part of the living medina. Simple street food and small cafés are only a few minutes’ walk away.
food.li1: Karan and barida from nearby stalls – the local classic.
food.li2: Fresh bread, olives and small grilled snacks.
food.li3: Mint tea in a quiet café just outside the busiest lanes.
food.li4: If you continue deeper into the medina, more grill and snail options appear.
food.li5: For a proper meal, head toward Place du 16 Août or the modern centre after your visit.
food.p2: Nothing is tourist-oriented here; you eat what locals eat. Prices are low and the experience is straightforward.

tips.title: Practical Tips for Visiting the Grande Mosquée

1.title: Getting There
1.desc: The mosque sits inside the medina, a short walk from Bab Sidi Abdelwahab or other main gates. Most taxi drivers know the area; ask for “Jamaa Al Kabir” or the Grande Mosquée.

2.title: Dress and Behaviour
2.desc: Dress modestly (shoulders and knees covered). Remove shoes only if invited inside a prayer area. Speak quietly and avoid blocking entrances.

3.title: Photography
3.desc: Exterior photos are generally fine. Always ask before photographing people. Do not photograph inside the prayer hall.

q1.question: Can non-Muslims enter the Grande Mosquée?
q1.answer: Non-Muslims may view the exterior and the area of the three fountains. Entry into the prayer hall is reserved for Muslims. Always respect any local instructions.

q2.question: What is the best time to visit?
q2.answer: Morning for soft light and fewer people, or late afternoon for golden light. Avoid the main prayer times if you want a quiet exterior visit.

q3.question: How long should I spend here?
q3.answer: 20 to 40 minutes is enough to see the exterior, the fountains and the surrounding lanes. It is a stop within a longer medina walk rather than a full half-day site.

q4.question: Is there an entrance fee?
q4.answer: No. Looking at the exterior and the fountains is free. There is no ticket office.

q5.question: Is photography allowed?
q5.answer: Exterior photography is generally accepted. Do not photograph worshippers without clear permission, and never inside the prayer area.
